newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada Sept unemployment seen bringing rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: Canada Sept unemployment seen bringing rate cuts.

text.p: A surge in unemployment in Canada to 9.9 percent in September means domestic demand in the country remains sluggish and the Bank of Canada will have to cut interest rates further to stimulate growth, economists said on Friday.

"This is disappointingly weak," said Andrew Spence, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "If you look at the elements of the report, all (the job losses) are pretty much in business services and this suggests to me that domestic demand remains pretty weak and that is confirmed because construction fell again in the month."
Spence said Canada's stubbornly high unemployment rate meant the Bank of Canada would need to ease interest rates further before signs of a lasting recovery in domestic demand could be seen.

"Today the Bank must think about not just offsetting some of the Canadian dollar appreciation we've seen over the last month or so, but whether or not to chart an outright easing policy again," Spence said.
"Cut, cut, cut. Cut rates. It's quite clear you've got to cut rates," he added.
Statistics Canada said on Friday that Canada's unemployment rate jumped to 9.9 percent in September from 9.4 percent in August as the economy lost 47,000 jobs.

"This report suggests to me that unless you see some evidence over the very near future that domestic demand is turning around, the Bank will also pursue probably another (cut of) 25 basis points," Spence said.

The Bank of Canada is expected to ease rates by 25 basis points this morning. The Bank would signal a rate cut by intervening in Canada's money markets, which it usually does around 0900 EDT/1300 GMT.

The Bank has cut rates by two percentage points so far this year and by 4.25 percentage points since May 1995. The last seven rate cuts were independent of the U.S. Federal Reserve. The last cut, on October 2, took the key overnight lending rate to a range of 3.50 to 4.0 percent and the Bank rate to 4.0 percent.
But the aggressive interest rate cutting seems to have done little to boost Canada's lagging economy.
"One gets the sense that the economy is just not living up to its potential," said Michael Gregory, economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers in Toronto.
Gregory said that the unemployment number for October would probably look even worse, due to the indirect impact of a continuing strike at General Motors' ) Canada unit.
"It's looking a little dismal out there and the economy just doesn't seem to be having that little bit of muster, that forward momentum," he said.
That means that lower interest rates are just around the corner, analysts said.
Gregory said that as long as interest rates in Canada remained above zero, there was room for more cuts.

"Let's put it this way: There was a time when Japanese overnight rates were 4.0 percent. And now they are 0.5 percent. How low can (rates) go? As long as they are positive, there is a chance they can go lower. Think Japan," Gregory said.

The economy's failure to create jobs will also backfire for Canada's Finance Minister Paul Martin, whose tough deficit reduction policies have been applauded by financial markets, but have been criticized by some politicians and businesses.
Martin will probably come under more pressure to cut taxes soon in a bid to create jobs, something he has resisted. Economists said he was likely to stay on his deficit-cutting path.

"(The unemployment number) does raise the specter of tax cuts. But given Martin's credibility and his comments just a couple of days ago, you've got to believe he is not thinking tax cuts," Gregory said.
--Malina Poshtova Zang, Reuters Ottawa Bureau (613) 235-6745
